extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy (Locke's theory of property and parental power)
extracted.subtask_short: Locke on property and parental power
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of John Locke's principles on the origin and limits of private property and the nature and limits of parental (paternal) authority, with examples and normative claims about labour, money, spoilage, and childhood. Sections discuss when appropriation is just, what bounds it, and how parental power is temporary.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man can give more power than he has himself
rubrics_metrics.description: No body can give more power than he has himself; he that cannot take away his own life cannot give another power over it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains limits on contractual surrender of fundamental rights: one cannot, by compact or consent, enslave oneself to the extent of giving another absolute arbitrary power to kill him. Even where one has forfeited his life by crime, the captor may defer taking it and use the person for service without injury; the captive may at any time resist and thereby draw on himself death if he prefers it to slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of slavery as a continued state of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery is nothing else but the state of war continued, between a lawful conqueror and a captive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a compact establishes limited power and obedience, the state of war/slavery ceases for the duration of that compact. This sets a criterion distinguishing absolute slavery from limited servitude: presence of arbitrary power vs. a mutually agreed limited condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale into servitude not equivalent to absolute slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical practices of selling oneself (e.g., among the Jews) were to drudgery, not to slavery, because the sold person was not under an absolute arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: masters were obliged to free servants after a term; maiming a servant (loss of eye/tooth) freed him (Exod. xxi.). This warns against conflating temporary bonded labour with permanent absolute domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: God gave the earth to mankind in common
rubrics_metrics.description: God ... has given the earth to the children of men; given it to mankind in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting premise for Locke's account of property: the earth as original common possession; subsequent private property must be explained from that starting point rather than assumed by exclusive grant to a single ancestor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property arises from mixing one's labour with common resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatsoever he removes out of the state that nature hath provided, and left it in, he hath mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and thereby makes it his property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by picking acorns, gathering apples, digging ore, catching fish, hunting hares: labour converts part of the commons into private property because labour is the unquestionable property of the labourer and annexes something of himself to the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation does not require express consent of all commoners
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking any part of what is common, and removing it out of the state nature leaves it in, which begins the property; the taking of this or that part, does not depend on the express consent of all the commoners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grass my horse has bit; turfs my servant cut; water in the pitcher belongs to him who drew it. Locke argues that requiring unanimous consent would make appropriation practically impossible and lead to starvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of appropriation: take only as much as one can use before it spoils
rubrics_metrics.description: As much as any one can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils, so much he may by his labour fix a property in; whatever is beyond this, is more than his share, and belongs to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This spoilage rule bounds legitimate appropriation: durable goods differ (money vs. perishable food). Hoarding perishable goods beyond use is unjust and a violation of the law of nature; use and non-spoilage determine permissible quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement (tillage, planting, cultivation) justifies enclosure of land
rubrics_metrics.description: As much land as a man tills, plants, improves, cultivates, and can use the product of, so much is his property. He by his labour does, as it were, inclose it from the common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labour expended in subduing or improving land annexes property; this appropriation is not invalidated by the fact that others have equal title in common, provided enough and as good are left for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of property set by extent of men's labour and conveniencies of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of property nature has well set by the extent of men’s labour and the conveniencies of life: no man’s labour could subdue, or appropriate all; nor could his enjoyment consume more than a small part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke appeals to practical limits: early possessions were moderate and unlikely to injure others; the natural measure restrains appropriation and reduces conflict while encouraging productive labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement increases common stock; enclosure can benefit mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: He that incloses land, and has a greater plenty of the conveniencies of life from ten acres, than he could have from an hundred left to nature, may truly be said to give ninety acres to mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that cultivation and industry make land far more productive; appropriation by improvement increases overall supplies and is thus justifiable and beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoilage of perishable goods in one's possession is a violation of the law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fruits rotted, or the venison putrified, before he could spend it, he offended against the common law of nature, and was liable to be punished; he invaded his neighbour’s share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession beyond one's ability to use causes waste and harms others by depriving them of resources they could use; proper use or disposition (e.g., gift, trade) prevents this violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money changes the limits of legitimate possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention of money, and the tacit agreement of men to put a value on it, introduced (by consent) larger possessions, and a right to them; ... gold and silver ... have its value only from the consent of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because money does not spoil and can be hoarded, a tacit consent to its use allows accumulation beyond what one can immediately use; this explains the unequal distribution of land in societies using money and shifts prior natural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour is the principal source of value
rubrics_metrics.description: It is labour indeed that puts the difference of value on every thing; ... in most of them ninety-nine hundredths are wholly to be put on the account of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke traces the value of bread, wine, cloth, etc., to the cumulative labour (not just nature) required for production and the many instruments and prior industries that contribute to final goods; this supports property claims grounded in labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation was originally non-prejudicial where plenty remained
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor was this appropriation of any parcel of land, by improving it, any prejudice to any other man, since there was still enough, and as good left; ... he that leaves as much as another can make use of, does as good as take nothing at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's justificatory constraint: appropriation acceptable where it leaves others as well off, i.e., enough and as good remaining; this is a fairness constraint on property acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original communities could settle boundaries and property by compact
rubrics_metrics.description: When they incorporated, settled themselves together, and built cities; and then, by consent, they came in time, to set out the bounds of their distinct territories, and agree on limits between them and their neighbours; and by laws within themselves, settled the properties of those of the same society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive law and compact within societies can fix property rules and boundaries beyond the natural-law labour-basis; historical emergence of municipal property regimes is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness and non-spoilage determine rightful exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: If he also bartered away plums, that would have rotted in a week, for nuts that would last good for his eating a whole year, he did no injury; he wasted not the common stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible exchanges that convert perishable goods into durable goods (or vice versa) are legitimate so long as they do not waste the common stock; trade can legitimately modify distribution within natural-law limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power is parental (mother and father) and not exclusively paternal
rubrics_metrics.description: This of paternal power ... seems so to place the power of parents over their children wholly in the father, as if the mother had no share in it; whereas, if we consult reason or revelation, we shall find, she hath an equal title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic and normative correction: the proper term should be 'parental' to reflect equal authority and obligations of both parents as indicated by scripture and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority is temporary and grows weaker as children mature
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ... are not born in this full state of equality, though they are born to it. Their parents have a sort of rule and jurisdiction over them ... but it is but a temporary one. The bonds of this subjection ... age and reason as they grow up, loosen them, till at length they drop quite off, and leave a man at his own free disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental power exists to preserve, nourish, and educate until children attain age and reason; its justification is remedial and protective, not absolute or perpetual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law binds only those to whom it is promulgated by reason
rubrics_metrics.description: No body can be under a law, which is not promulgated to him; and this law being promulgated or made known by reason only, he that is not come to the use of his reason, cannot be said to be under this law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim about the nature of law: law is direction of a free and intelligent agent made known by reason; infants lacking use of reason are not directly subject to this law, justifying parental jurisdiction until reason arrives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental obligation arises from the child's helplessness and is accountable to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam and Eve, and after them all parents were, by the law of nature, under an obligation to preserve, nourish, and educate the children they had begotten; not as their own workmanship, but the workmanship of their own maker, the Almighty, to whom they were to be accountable for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental power is grounded in duty to preserve and raise offspring who are born weak and helpless; parents are stewards accountable to divine and natural law for their children's upbringing.
